log.action: I approach the refugees and ask where they came from and what burned. I also ask who runs things in Marrowgate — who I'd talk to about work, and where they can be found in town.
log.narration: Turn 1The refugees flinch when you step close. Burned people always do. One of them, a broad woman with a seared forearm and hollow eyes, decides you look less dangerous than the alternatives."Ashfen," she says. "Upriver. Three days gone." She does not elaborate. She does not need to. The smell does it for her.A younger man beside her, head wrapped in cloth, spits toward the water. "Something came out of the Reach. At night. Fire, but wrong. Too controlled. Too deliberate." He looks at your hands, then back at your face. He does not say what he is thinking. He does not have to.You ask about work. Who runs things here.The woman almost laughs. "Counting House, on the main street. A man named Sorn owns half the debt in this town. If you want work, he is where the coin flows from." She pauses. "If you want honest work, try the watch captain. Wyndfall. Keeps an office near the gate."🔊………

log.action: No point walking all that way if the man has no use for me. I cast Message at Sorn in his Counting House on the main street — a whisper across town to ask whether he has work for a sorcerer who is not particular.
log.narration: Turn 2Message doesn't work like that. The Counting House is the length of a town away, well past a hundred and twenty feet, and the spell needs a clear line to a specific creature you can see. Sorn is a name, not a face. The whisper dies before it leaves your throat.The refugees are still watching you. The woman's expression hasn't changed. She has seen stranger failures today.The Counting House isn't going anywhere. Neither is the watch captain's office. But something else moves at the edge of the dock crowd, a figure cutting against the flow of refugees with the practiced ease of someone who belongs nowhere and everywhere. A hood, a satchel, the particular walk of a person who is listening harder than they are moving. They glance back once. At you, specifically.🔊………

log.action: I cut through the crowd after the hooded figure. When I'm close I say, low: 'You walk like someone who listens for a living, and you looked at me like you know what these scars mean. I'm Vex Calder. If you're a practitioner, say so — I could use a partner in this town, and it seems there's work coming downriver.'
log.narration: Turn 3The figure stops. Doesn't run, which tells you something.They turn. A woman, middle-aged, with ink-stained fingers and eyes that have done a lot of calculating in their time. No obvious weapons. The satchel hangs heavy, though. Books, maybe, or something that wants to be kept quiet."Davin," she says, which is clearly not her name. A placeholder. A test.She looks at the scars on your hands the way a smith looks at a blade, checking the work, checking the origin. Her jaw tightens a fraction."Practitioner is a generous word for what I am." She glances at the refugees behind you. "And you are either very confident or very stupid to say a name like Calder out loud on a dock like this." She lets that sit. "Who told you there was work coming downriver?"🔊………

log.action: 'Nobody told me. A barge full of burned people told me — trouble like that always turns into paid work for people like us. I mean to see the watch captain about it. Come with me. Equal split, and I don't ask what's in the satchel.' I offer my scarred hand to seal it.
log.narration: Turn 4She looks at the hand. Looks at it for a while.Then she takes it. Her grip is firm and dry and she shakes once, the way people do when they have learned from experience that a soft grip invites renegotiation."Equal split," she says. "And you don't ask about the satchel." She does not repeat your terms as agreement. She repeats them as a contract. There is a difference, and she knows it.She falls into step beside you without being asked. The crowd parts a little. Burned refugees, dock workers, a pair of watch soldiers who look at the two of you and decide there are easier problems tonight."The captain is going to ask how you got here," she says, quietly, watching the gate ahead. "And he is going to ask about the fire. Men with scars like yours and fire in their hands make nervous captains very curious." A pause. "I would have a story ready. Something simple. Simple lies hold longer."She says it like someone who has told a few.🔊………

log.action: We walk to the watch captain's office by the river gate. I tell Wyndfall straight: 'Captain, you have a dock full of burned refugees and worse coming behind them, I'd wager. I'm a sorcerer, my partner has her own talents. Give us something bounded and paid — a job we can finish tonight — and we'll show you what we're worth.'
log.narration: Turn 5Wyndfall's office smells of tallow and old boot leather. The man himself is broad across the shoulders, going grey at the temples, with the flat eyes of someone who has stopped being surprised by anything the river brings. He listens to you without moving. That is either patience or contempt. Hard to say which."Tonight," he repeats. Flat. He looks at Celeste, then back at you.He stands, moves to the narrow window overlooking the dock. The refugees are still there, huddled against the pilings in the torchlight."One of those people says they saw a man walking out of the fire at Ashfen. Upright. Unhurried." He turns back. "Not burned. Not running. Walking." He lets that land. "I want to know if that man came downriver with them. I want to know if he is in my town right now. Find him. Don't kill him. Bring him to me breathing."He drops a small purse on the desk between you. Doesn't push it toward you. Leaves it there, so you have to reach."Ten gold if you find him. Five if you find a body."🔊………

log.action: 'Breathing. Understood. We'll take it.' I pocket nothing yet — payment on delivery. Back at the dock, I ask Celeste to work the refugees with me: who saw the walking man, what did he look like, and did anyone see where the barge passengers scattered to once they landed.
log.narration: Turn 6Wyndfall nods once. Deal made.Back at the dock the torches are burning lower and the refugees have spread thin, some already swallowed by the town's cheaper alleys. You work fast. Celeste takes the left side of the crowd, quiet and methodical, her cloak hood down so she looks less like a threat. You take the right.It takes twenty minutes and costs you nothing but patience.Three people saw the man. Their descriptions align well enough to be useful. Tall. Lean. Hair gone white at the front, not from age. Wearing what used to be a coat. He stepped off the barge without speaking to anyone and walked up the main thoroughfare without looking back. One old man, shaking hard, says the fire at Ashfen bent toward the walking man. Bent toward him, not away.Celeste finds you at the waterline. "A dockworker saw him go into the Tallow Quarter," she says quietly. "The cheap lodging district, north off the main street. Didn't come back out." She pauses. "He also says the man bought a meat pie and paid in ash-blackened coin." She says it like it means something. It probably does.🔊………

log.action: We head north into the Tallow Quarter after the white-haired man. I keep my staff loose in my hand and watch the alley mouths — word travels fast in a town like this, and I said the name Calder out loud on a crowded dock.
log.narration: Turn 7The Tallow Quarter earns its name. Candle-renders and knackers and three kinds of business that don't advertise. The streets narrow fast, the buildings leaning in like they're listening. Grease on the cobbles. Something dead nearby, not quite recent enough to smell but close.You watch the alley mouths. Good instinct.Because someone is watching you back.A figure, doorway left, thirty feet behind. Moves when you move. Stops when you stop. Not a drunk. Not a lost refugee. The posture is too deliberate. Hood up, hands low.Celeste says nothing. She has already noticed. A slight angle to her shoulder tells you so.The quarter opens briefly into a small square, a tallow-lamp guttering at its centre, three alleys branching off it like broken fingers. And there, at the far end of the square near the entrance to a cheap lodging house, a man sits on a stone step eating what remains of a meat pie.Tall. Lean. Hair white at the front.He is not looking at you. He is looking at the lamp flame. The flame is leaning toward him. Just slightly. The way a dog leans toward a familiar hand.Behind you, the shadow in the doorway has not moved.🔊………

log.action: I turn my back on the pie-eater and face the doorway shadow square on, staff up, flame licking along my knuckles so the whole square can see it. 'You've been on us since the dock. Sorn's coin, I'd wager. Come out — and tell your friends in the alleys to come out too. I won't ask twice.'
log.narration: Turn 8The flame on your knuckles throws orange light across the square. Everything stops. A knacker's apprentice across the way finds something urgent to do inside.The figure steps out.A woman. Sharp-faced, dark-eyed, dressed for not being noticed. She is not reaching for a weapon. That is either confidence or calculation. Possibly both.She looks at your fire. Then at you. Then at Celeste, briefly, the way a person takes inventory."Sorn's coin," she repeats. Quiet amusement, no teeth in it. "You said that name loud enough for the whole quarter to hear. Brave. Or careless." She tilts her head. "Which is it?"She does not come out of the alleys. Because there is nobody in the alleys. She came alone. That is either very confident or very stupid, and she does not look stupid."My name is Thessa Quelrath," she says, as if that should mean something. "And I have been watching you since the dock because you walked straight toward the most dangerous man in this quarter without knowing what he is." She glances past you at the white-haired figure on the steps, still eating, still bending the flame. "So before you go any further. I thought someone should ask." A pause. "Do you actually know what you are walking toward?"🔊………

log.action: 'I know the watch wants him breathing, and that's the job.' I let the knuckle-flame die, nod Celeste to circle wide, and walk toward the white-haired man, open-handed. 'Friend. The watch captain wants a word about Ashfen. You can walk with us easy, or this square gets loud. Your choice.'
log.narration: Turn 9Celeste moves. Quiet, wide arc, cutting off the alley to the right.Thessa doesn't follow. She stays exactly where she is, arms folded, watching with the expression of someone who has seen this go badly before and is waiting to be proven right.The white-haired man finishes his meat pie. Folds the paper it came in. Sets it on the step beside him with the care of a man who has nowhere urgent to be.Then he looks up at you.His eyes are wrong. Not the colour. The depth. Like looking down a well and not hearing the stone hit water."Ashfen," he says. His voice is low and even and carries no grief at all. "I watched it burn for two hours before I left." He studies your open hands. Studies the staff. Studies the faint scorch still on your knuckles. Something shifts in his expression. Recognition, maybe. Or assessment. "You have fire in your blood," he says. Not a question. "Real fire. Not a trick."He stands. Slowly. He is very tall."I will walk with you," he says. "But not because of the watch captain."Behind you, Thessa says something very quiet."That is exactly what I was afraid of."🔊………

log.action: 'Good enough. Walk.' We take him back toward the river gate, Celeste on his left, me on his right, through the narrow greasy streets. I keep count of every shadow — a man like Sorn hears a name like Calder said on his own dock, and he doesn't send one polite woman to ask questions, he sends collectors mob-handed.
log.narration: Turn 10Smart thinking. Wrong night to stop.You make the first turning without trouble. Second too. The Tallow Quarter thins out, cheaper lodgings giving way to storage yards and a cooper's workshop, dark and shuttered.Third turning.Four men step out ahead. Not refugees. Not drunks. Work-boots, short clubs, the flat patience of men paid to wait in the cold. One has a lantern. He holds it up, looks at the three of you, looks at the tall white-haired man between you."The sorcerer," he says. Conversational. "Wyndfall's dog, we hear. Leave the old man. Walk away. Captain gets nothing tonight."Behind you, footsteps. Two more, cutting off the retreat.Six total. Clubs, at least one blade on the lantern-holder's hip. No crossbows visible, which is the only good news.The white-haired man, Rhett, says nothing. He is watching the lantern flame. It is leaning toward him again, straining against the wick.Celeste's hand moves under her cloak. Her lips are pressed thin.Thessa is gone. Slipped away somewhere in the last block. Of course she has.Six to three, in a dark street, and the nearest watch post is four minutes away.🔊………

log.action: No speeches. I pull the Flask of Alchemist's Fire from my coat and hurl it at the cobbles between the two men cutting off our retreat — let it burst and burn, and let the whole street see what happens when you corner a fire-sorcerer. Then I shout to Celeste: 'The lantern man is yours — put him down!'
log.narration: Turn 11Dexterity saving throwd20: 7 -- failedDexterity saving throwd20: 14 -- successDexterity saving throwd20: 6 -- failedThe flask spins end over end and shatters on the cobblestones.Blue-white fire blooms across the street behind you. Both blockers jump back. One catches his boot-heel in the gutter and goes down hard. The other scrambles into a doorway, trousers smoking, all his courage suddenly elsewhere.Rear threat, neutralised. For now.Celeste doesn't wait to be told twice. Her hand comes out from under her cloak empty, and then light falls on the lantern holder like a judgement. Sacred flame, dropping straight down, no cover in the world helping him.He takes it full. Staggers. The lantern swings wild, oil sloshing.Four club thugs remain ahead, and the one in the doorway might find his nerve again. Rhett stands between you both, hands loose at his sides. The lantern flame is nearly horizontal now, straining toward him like a compass needle finding north.He has not moved. He is smiling faintly.🔊………

log.action: The one in the doorway with the smoking trousers — he's reaching for his nerve again. I don't let him find it. Fire Bolt, straight at his chest, and I name him for Celeste: 'Doorway man is getting back up!' Then I set my back to Rhett and face the four with clubs.
log.narration: Turn 12Ranged spell attackd20: 17 -- hitClub Thug attack vs Vexd20: 11 -- missClub Thug attack vs Vexd20: 8 -- missClub Thug attack vs Celested20: 13 -- hitThe Fire Bolt takes the doorway man square in the sternum.He folds back into the doorway and stays there. Not dead. Not getting up either. The alchemist's fire still gutters between you and the second rear blocker, and he has found something very important to stare at in the middle distance.Four ahead. They look at each other. Men with clubs always look at each other at moments like this, checking who is going to be brave first. Nobody wants to be brave first.Then one of them decides. Rushes you.The others follow, because that is how mobs work.Clumsy. Scared. They swing wide and you let them, feet moving, keeping Rhett behind you. One catches your shoulder with a glancing blow, no real weight in it.The lantern holder is still standing. Barely. Celeste put radiance through him and he is running on stubbornness alone. He draws the blade on his hip, slow and deliberate, and points it at you.Nine feet. Inside Fire Lance range.Celeste hisses. A club finds her ribs.🔊………

log.action: They want to mob a sorcerer in a narrow street — fine. Scorching Ray: three lances of fire, one into each of the front rushers. I burn the spell hot and I make it THEATRE, because I want the ones behind to watch their friends burn and think hard about their wages.
log.narration: Turn 13Scorching Ray attack 1d20: 19 -- hitScorching Ray attack 2d20: 12 -- hitScorching Ray attack 3d20: 8 -- missLantern Holder attack vs Vexd20: 16 -- hitThree rays, one after another, cracking out of your palm like whip-strikes.Two connect. The first thug takes it in the shoulder and spins, coat alight, screaming in a way that carries. The second catches it across the face. He drops without ceremony. Just drops.The third ray scorches a black line across the cobblestones. Close enough.The street smells of burning wool and scorched hair. The standing thugs look at their friends. One is rolling on the ground, slapping at his coat. One is not moving at all.The theatre works. You can see it happen, the moment the calculation changes behind their eyes. Clubs versus fire. Wages versus this.The lantern holder does not run. He is either braver or more desperate than the rest. He comes at you, blade low, and he knows how to hold it.Cold pain across your forearm. A real cut. Blood on your sleeve.The two remaining club thugs look at each other again.🔊………

log.action: I raise my hand, flame curling between my fingers, and give them the way out: 'Drop the clubs. Take your burned friends and walk, and tell Sorn the price of the old man just went up past what he pays you. Next one who swings, I stop aiming at coats.'
log.narration: Turn 14Charisma check — Intimidationd20: 15 -- successThe clubs hit the cobblestones. Both of them. Almost at the same time.Nobody wants to be the example. They already have two examples. Both examples are on the ground making bad sounds.The lantern holder looks at you. Looks at the flame between your fingers. Looks at the two examples. He sheathes the blade. Slow, deliberate, like he is making a point about not being afraid, even though he absolutely is.They gather their burned friends. Nobody speaks. One of them has to carry the man who dropped and does it with the mechanical efficiency of someone who has done this before, which is its own kind of information about Sorn's operation.They go.The alchemist's fire is dying on the cobblestones, guttering blue at the edges. The street is empty. Quiet, except for wind and the distant sound of the river.Rhett sits back down on his step. Picks up what remains of his meat pie. Takes a bite."Sorn," he says, conversationally. "That name keeps coming up."Celeste is pressing a hand to her ribs, breathing carefully. Not collapsed. Not complaining. Just filing it away.Your arm is bleeding steadily into your sleeve. It needs binding before Wyndfall sees it.🔊………

log.action: The street empties and I finally feel it — the lantern man's blade caught me across the ribs and every breath drags. I ask Celeste: 'That arm of yours took a club. Mend yourself first — properly, the real prayer, not the little trick — then look at my ribs. I think something's cracked.'
log.narration: Turn 15Celeste looks at you. Then at her own ribs. Then back at you."Mine are bruised. Yours are bleeding." She does not wait for further instruction.Her hands find the cut on your forearm first, not your ribs. You start to object. She ignores you with the practiced ease of someone who has ignored many objections. Her iron symbol comes out from under her collar, and she speaks something low and without performance, a working prayer, not theatre.Warmth moves through the wound. The bleeding slows. Not gone, but manageable."Ribs are bruised," she says, pressing two fingers below your left side with clinical dispassion. "Not cracked. You would know if they were cracked."Rhett watches this from his step. He has finished the meat pie. He folds the paper it came in with quiet neatness and tucks it into his coat."The watch captain," he says. "That is where you are taking me."Not a question."Yes," you say."Wyndfall." He tries the name like a man tasting something unfamiliar. "I have heard worse names."He stands. Steady on his feet. The lantern on the wall behind him gutters and bends toward his back as he turns away from it.🔊………

log.action: 'The job is not done until he is standing in Wyndfall's office, breathing, like the man said. The Burning Man is still our contract — keep it live in your head, Celeste.' We take Rhett the rest of the way to the watch captain's office and hand him over.
log.narration: Turn 16The river gate watch post smells of tallow and damp wool. Wyndfall is already there when you arrive, which means his man ran fast. He looks at Rhett. Looks at your arm. Looks at Celeste pressing a careful hand to her side. His expression does not change."That him?""That's him," you say.Wyndfall studies Rhett for a long moment. Rhett studies him back. Neither man blinks first. It is not a comfortable silence."You walked out of Ashfen," Wyndfall says. Flat. A statement, not a question."I walked out of many places," Rhett says.Wyndfall lets that sit. Then he reaches into his coat and puts ten gold on the desk between you without ceremony or gratitude."Wait outside," he tells Rhett. Two guards materialise from somewhere and flank him. Rhett goes without complaint, which is either cooperation or confidence. Hard to read.Wyndfall looks at you. "Sorn's people hit you in the Tallow Quarter." Again, not a question. Word travels fast in a small town, apparently.His jaw works once. Something is coming. Something he does not entirely want to say.🔊………

log.action: I take the gold and pocket it. 'One more thing, Captain — half the Tallow Quarter watched me burn Sorn's collectors off a corner tonight. By morning there'll be a story with my name stitched to it. What are they calling me? I'd rather hear it from you than from a broadsheet.'
log.narration: Turn 17Wyndfall's mouth does something that is not quite a smile."They are calling you the Northlander." He says it like it is already a title. "Word has Sorn's boys running from a fire-witch with a foreign accent." He pauses. "Some versions have you eight feet tall.""Flattering," you say."It is a problem," he says. "Sorn knows your face now. Knows your name, probably. He does not send collectors twice at the same man. He sends something worse."He moves to the window. The dock is quiet. The refugee barge sits dark against the pilings."I had a report this afternoon," he says, slower now. Choosing words. "Another burning. Not Ashfen. A waystation in the Reach, two days east. Same pattern. Controlled. Deliberate." He turns. "Whoever walked out of Ashfen, he did not start the fire. He just watched it."That lands differently than he intends it to.He looks at Rhett's empty chair. Then at you."I need someone to ride out to that waystation before the trail goes cold. Someone Sorn cannot follow through official channels." A pause. "Same rate. Plus expenses."Outside, through the thin wall, you can hear Rhett breathing. Steady. Unhurried.🔊………

log.action: 'The Northlander.' I turn the word over and find I like the weight of it. 'Then that's who burned Sorn's crew — not Vex Calder. Let the town stitch the story to the title. I'll wear it.' I tell Celeste and Wyndfall both: from tonight, in Marrowgate, I answer to the Northlander.
log.narration: Turn 18Wyndfall looks at you for a moment. Then he writes something in his ledger. Does not say what.Celeste says nothing either. She has that look, the one that means she is filing the information away somewhere you will not find it."The Northlander," Wyndfall repeats. Flat. Professional. "Right."It is not endorsement. It is not mockery. It is a man deciding the name costs him nothing and might cost Sorn something, and making his calculation accordingly.Smart man."The waystation," he says. "Do you want the job or not?"Outside, one of the guards says something low to Rhett. Rhett does not respond. The silence from that room has a particular quality to it, the silence of a man who is deciding something, and has been deciding it since before you walked him through the door.Your arm aches where Celeste bound it. The gold sits heavy in your pocket, ten pieces that already feel spent. Sorn knows your face. His next move will not be clubs and lanterns.Two days east, a waystation burned the same way Ashfen burned.The same pattern. The same hand, maybe.Wyndfall waits. He is good at waiting.🔊………

log.action: Outside the watch post, while Celeste checks her satchel straps, I speak quietly — to myself as much as to her, barely above the river noise: 'Equal split was the contract. But after tonight, it's more than a contract. I'm sworn to see you through this alive, whatever's burning its way downriver.' I don't wait for an answer; I start walking toward the inn.
log.narration: Turn 19She hears it. She does not pretend otherwise.Her hands slow on the buckles. One beat. Two.Then the straps are tight and she falls into step beside you, half a pace back, the way she always walks. Like she learned early to let someone else be first through a door."Sworn," she says. Quiet. Tasting the word the same way you tasted Northlander. "That is a specific thing to say."You keep walking. River noise fills the gap."I know what it costs you," she says. Not soft. Just accurate. "A man who cannot leave a debt unpaid, swearing oaths. You are building a cage out of your own principles."She is not wrong. She is irritatingly not wrong.The town is dark past the watch post, torches burned low, the cold wind pushing ash across the cobbles. Somewhere in the Tallow Quarter, Sorn's men are counting their burned friends and composing a report. Somewhere behind a wall, Rhett Lorrath sits in a chair and decides things quietly.Celeste pulls her cloak tighter."Equal split," she says finally. "And you stay alive long enough to honour it."Not acceptance. Not refusal. Something in between that functions like both.🔊………

log.action: We find the least rotten inn near the gate — the one with a stable and a door that bars. I pay for two rooms and hot food, and we take the night: full rest, spells and all. Tomorrow we decide about the waystation job.
log.narration: Turn 20The inn is called the Silt & Board. Nobody is proud of it.Two rooms, hot broth, bread that was fresh sometime this week. The barkeep is a dwarf woman with a scar through one eyebrow and the particular incuriosity of someone who has learned not to ask names. You pay without haggling. Tonight is not the night to count copper.Your room is small. The bar on the door is solid. That is enough.You eat. You sleep. The arm aches less by morning.Celeste is already at the common room table when you come down, both hands wrapped around a clay cup, her satchel between her feet where she can feel it. She looks like she slept the way soldiers sleep. Adequately. Without peace.She glances up."Waystation," she says. Not a question.Outside, pale light. Cold. The ash smell is worse in the morning, when the wind drops and the Reach breathes in.Two days east. A burned building and whatever it left behind.Wyndfall's coin in your pocket. Sorn's patience running thin somewhere across the quarter.🔊………

log.action: Wyndfall said Sorn doesn't send collectors twice — he sends something worse. So before we leave for any waystation, I settle it. I step out of the Silt & Board into the dawn street, deliberately visible, and wait for whatever Sorn sent to find me. Celeste watches the rooftops from the doorway.
log.narration: Turn 21Bold. Possibly stupid. Hard to tell yet.The street is quiet. Pre-dawn quiet, the kind with weight to it. A carter somewhere, wheels on stone. A dog that has given up barking. The ash smell sits flat on the cold air.You wait.Three minutes. Five.Then a boy, no, not a boy. A small figure. Gnome, male, narrow-shouldered, dressed in the drab brown of someone paid to be forgettable. He walks straight toward you with the unhurried ease of a man who was never going to sneak. Stops six feet out. Looks up at you with pale eyes that have done a great deal of arithmetic.He holds out a folded letter. Sealed in grey wax. No crest. Just a thumbprint pressed into it."From Aldric Sorn," he says. Voice like dry paper. "He asks that you read it before you leave the city."Celeste has gone very still in the doorway.The gnome does not move. Does not fidget. He has delivered a hundred letters like this one, at dawn, to men standing in streets trying to look unbothered. He will stand there until you take it or until you burn him, and he seems comfortable with either outcome.🔊………

log.action: I break the grey wax and read the letter where the gnome can watch my face. Whatever it offers or threatens, my answer is the same: 'Tell Sorn the Northlander's debt is not for sale, and neither is the old man.' Then Celeste and I take the east road out of Marrowgate toward the burned waystation, watching the treeline.
log.narration: Turn 22The letter is short. Sorn writes like a man who has never needed more than a few lines.Northlander,You have something that belongs to my interests. The old man is incidental. What I want is the fire. Come and discuss terms before the Reach takes you. I am a reasonable creditor.A.S.P.S. The name Calder is an interesting one. I have met it before, in ledgers.You fold it. Pocket it. The gnome watches your face and finds nothing useful there."Tell Sorn the Northlander's debt is not for sale," you say. "Neither is the old man."The gnome nods. No surprise. No reaction. He turns and walks back the way he came, already composing the reply in his head.Celeste is at your shoulder before he rounds the corner."He knows your name," she says."He knows a name," you say.She lets that sit for exactly one step. Then, "That letter changes the waystation job."It does. You both know it.The east road out of Marrowgate is hard-packed mud gone grey with frost. The Reach opens up fast past the walls, scrub and black water and skeleton trees pressing in from both sides. No birdsong. The ash smell thickens the further you walk.Something burned this way. Not long ago.🔊………

log.action: We push east along the river road through the Reach, hard pace, open stretches where nothing can come at us unseen. Ashfen's refugees came down this road — which means whatever preys on refugees is still working it. I keep my staff in hand and watch the ditches and the treeline both.
log.narration: Turn 23Perception checkd20: 15 -- successSmart. The Reach rewards attention and punishes comfort.The road follows the river, mostly. Brown water to the left, slow and flat. The treeline to the right is close enough that something patient could wait in it all day. The frost has not melted. By midmorning the sky is the colour of old linen and the light is doing nothing useful.You pass a shrine at a crossroads. Something old, pre-Marrowgate, a carved stone face worn down to a smear. Someone has left a bundle of rags at its base. On closer inspection, not rags.A coat. A child's shoe. Left in a hurry, or left as warning.Celeste crouches, touches the coat without lifting it. Her jaw is set."Three days old," she says. "Maybe four."Ashfen refugees came this way carrying what they had. Not everything made it.The ditch on your right is deep enough to hide a man lying flat. You watch it. Nothing moves. But fifty yards further the mud is disturbed, boot prints off the road into the scrub, several sets, and the grass between them is dark and matted.Not ash.Celeste sees it the same moment you do. log.action: We mark the shrine for the way back and press the pace — I want the waystation before full dark. When we get close I slow us to a hunter's walk and come at it from upwind, staff ready, watching for anything that survived the burning or anything that caused it.

That lands differently than he intends it to.

Charcoal. Rendered fat. Something underneath that you do not name.

The flame drops six feet and catches on something.

Not water. The well is dry. Has been dry long enough that the stones at the bottom are pale with old mineral crust.

What the flame catches on is paper. A bundle of it, oilcloth-wrapped, wedged into a crack in the shaft wall at arm's reach below the collar. Deliberate. Hidden by someone who expected to come back for it.

You note it. Leave it. The shaft is narrow but manageable.

Behind you, Celeste's voice. Careful and flat, the tone that means she is keeping something out of it.

"Vex."

You turn.

She is standing in the stable doorway. Not drawing her dagger. Not backing away. Just standing with a particular stillness that means she has assessed the situation and found it requires you.

Alive. Eyes open. Watching you both with the expression of a man who stopped expecting rescue two days ago and has not yet recalibrated.

He is not human. The ears are wrong. The jaw. Something faintly lupine in the bones of his face.

He says nothing. Waits to see what you are.

He does not startle. Does not reach for a blade.

He looks at the flame in your palm for a long moment. Something moves behind his eyes. Not fear. Recognition.

"Marrowgate," he says. Voice like gravel dragged slow. "How many days?"

"Two," you say.

He closes his eyes. Opens them. Does some arithmetic you are not party to.

"Then they have not reached it yet."

He shifts, hisses through his teeth, hand pressing harder against his thigh. The binding is soaked through. Dark and slow, which means deep but not arterial. He has been managing it alone in the cold for two days with horse blankets and strips of shirt and whatever stubbornness keeps a man alive when he has decided to stay that way.

"Who has not reached Marrowgate?" Celeste. She is in the doorway now, healer's kit already unstrapped from her satchel.

He looks at her. Then back at you.

"The ones who set this fire," he says. "They were not finished here. They left something behind." He jerks his chin toward the yard. Toward the well. "In the shaft. They do not know I watched them hide it."

His jaw is tight with pain. His eyes are steady.

The shaft is cold and close and smells of old stone and nothing else.

You brace your back against one side, boots against the other, and work down in short drops. The mineral crust is dry and solid enough to hold a boot. The crack is exactly where the flame showed it, south-facing, chest height from the bottom. Whoever hid this was not tall.

The oilcloth is tied with waxed cord. Three knots, tight, done by someone who expected weather rather than a dry shaft. You work it loose with your teeth and one hand while the other keeps you wedged.

Getting back up is uglier than going down.

You emerge into the cold with barked knuckles and ash on your coat and the bundle under your arm.

The stable. Celeste is cutting away Knox's improvised binding with the focused quiet of someone who has learned not to react to wounds. Knox is watching the ceiling and breathing through his nose.

You sit on a scorched beam and unwrap the oilcloth.

Inside: three things.

A map. Hand-drawn on heavy paper, Marrowgate marked with a circle, three other points marked with a symbol you do not recognise. A spiral. Tight, deliberate, the kind drawn by someone who has drawn it many times before.

A list of names. Twelve of them. Yours is not among them. But Wyndfall's is.

And a tooth. Large. Not human.

Knox speaks from the stable floor, leg newly bound and colour returning to his face.

"Bold," he says. "Possibly stupid. Hard to tell yet."

"That is usually how it goes," Celeste says. She is already moving, cloak pulled close, positioning herself at the corner where the road bends into sight.

You get Knox settled. Small fire, shielded by collapsed timber so the light does not bleed past the stable walls. He does not complain about the cold or the pain. The kind of man who has learned those are permanent conditions.

The bundle goes on the well collar. Oilcloth retied. Three knots, approximate.

Then you find your shadow behind the standing wall and you wait.

The Reach does not make sound at night. No insects. The burned ground kills that. Wind moves through the char in a way that sounds like breathing if you listen too long, so you stop listening.

An hour. Maybe more.

Then a boot on gravel. Careful. One person, moving slow from the treeline. They pause at the yard's edge. Assess. The bundle on the collar pulls their eye exactly as intended.

They move for it.

Short. Hooded. The walk is deliberate, unhurried. Someone who has done careful things before.

They reach for the oilcloth.

They freeze.

Both hands on the bundle. The firelight catches the hood, catches the breath misting in the cold air. A long pause. The kind where a person runs the numbers.

Then, slowly, they set the bundle back on the collar and raise both hands.

The hood comes down on its own, which is either cooperation or theatre.

A woman. Older, fifties maybe, sharp-faced and weathered in the way the Reach weathers everything, relentlessly and without apology. A scar along the left jaw, old enough to be white. Eyes that move between you and Celeste and back with quick professional assessment.

"The knots," she says. "I should have used four."

No fear in her voice. Irritation, mostly. At herself.

Celeste is behind her, eight feet, dagger drawn but low.

"Who are you?" you say.

You do not answer. Neither does she, yet.

"The names on that list," she says. "I was trying to warn them."

Her hands stay up. Her eyes stay steady. She is telling the truth or she is very good at this, and those are not mutually exclusive.
